specAnchors.text: understand that polarisation of anions by cations leads to some covalency in an ionic bond, based on evidence from the Born-Haber cycle

primer.text: Theoretical lattice energies assume perfectly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attraction. When a small, highly charged cation distorts a large anion's electron cloud, covalent character creeps in and measured values become more exothermic than predicted. This note ranks polarising power from charge density and polarisability from ionic radius.

modules.title: When perfect ionic model meets reality
modules.opening: Theoretical lattice energies assume perfectly spherical ions with purely electrostatic attraction. Real cations distort the electron clouds of nearby anions - polarisation - and the resulting covalent character makes measured values more exothermic than the theory predicts. Small, highly charged cations distort hardest.
keyPoints: Theoretical lattice energies assume 100% spherical ions with purely electrostatic attractions and whole-number charge exchange.
Polarisation occurs when the cation attracts electrons from the anion, distorting the anion's electron density and introducing covalent character.
Distorted lattices therefore show measured lattice energies more exothermic than the theoretical values.
A cation's polarising power rises with charge density - charge divided by surface area - so small, highly charged cations polarise most.
K+ has lower polarising power than Li+ (larger radius), and Na+ has lower than Mg2+ (smaller charge).

low.restatement: Theoretical values assume perfect spheres; real small, highly charged cations pull anion electrons inward, adding covalent character and deepening measured values.
low.analogy: A strong magnet warping a loose shower curtain: the curtain (anion cloud) bulges toward the magnet (cation).
low.examPointer: When measured beats theoretical, say 'polarisation' and name the small, highly charged cation.

medium.restatement: Charge density is the lever: the same charge squeezed into a smaller sphere pulls harder on the anion's cloud, and that pull is covalency creeping in.
medium.analogy: The same weight on a stiletto heel dents a floor that a flat shoe leaves untouched.
medium.examPointer: Compare pairs by both charge and radius before ranking polarising power.

modules.title: Anions that yield easily
sourceHeadings: Comparing the Covalent Character of NaCl and MgCl<sub>2</sub>
modules.opening: Anions are the passive partner: their polarisability tracks ionic radius, so large electron clouds yield easily. Bromide distorts more readily than chloride, and the NaCl versus MgCl2 comparison shows both levers at once - the 2+ magnesium cation pulls harder, so magnesium chloride carries the greater covalent character.
keyPoints: Anions are polarised, and their polarisability depends on ionic radius.
A bigger ionic radius lets the anion distort more easily, which is why Br- is more polarisable than Cl-.
Charge density can be approximated as charge divided by the square of the ionic radius to estimate covalent character.
In the NaCl versus MgCl2 comparison, the Mg2+ cation polarises Cl- more strongly than Na+ does, giving MgCl2 the greater covalent character.

low.restatement: Big anions polarise easily (Br- over Cl-); the cation's charge density decides the pull, so MgCl2 shows more covalent character than NaCl.
low.analogy: A large soap bubble bursts at a touch while a tight balloon resists: size is vulnerability.
low.examPointer: Pair-comparison questions want both names - which cation, which anion - before the verdict.

medium.restatement: Polarisability is the anion's softness: a diffuse outer cloud holds its electrons loosely, and any nearby charge reshapes it.
medium.analogy: A jelly wobbles at a footstep while a marble ignores it.
medium.examPointer: When comparing two compounds, vary one factor at a time - cation charge or anion radius - and state which.

glossary.definition: The distortion of an anion's electron cloud by a nearby cation, adding covalent character.
A cation's ability to distort anions, rising with charge density.
An anion's susceptibility to distortion, rising with ionic radius.
